transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, so, what brings me in... well, it's a lot of things, I guess, but mostly it's just been getting to this point where I feel like I absolutely cannot settle in my own body anymore. It’s the strangest feeling, almost like there’s a motor running inside me that I can’t switch off. 

And it really flares up, like, especially when I’m supposed to just sit quietly and do the things I need to do—like handling the household paperwork or sitting down to go over shared household plans. My husband will want to sit at the dining table on a Sunday morning and just figure out the week, look at the bills, you know, normal adult stuff, and I just... I can't sit there. I'm shifting in my chair, I'm getting up to grab a glass of water, I'm tapping my foot, and it feels physically uncomfortable to just be still and focus on the paper in front of me. 

I mean, I have a bachelor's degree, I used to be able to push through this kind of stuff when I was younger, but lately, being at home and trying to manage the day-to-day admin of our lives... it's like my body is just rebelling against sitting quietly. I just feel so restless all the time, like I have to be up and doing something, anything, other than sitting there looking at those plans. And it's exhausting, honestly, because I want to just be able to sit and get it done, but I just can't seem to make my body cooperate.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Act on impulse... hmm. No, honestly, I don't think I do. It’s actually kind of the opposite, in a way? 

Like, I know I just said my body is always going, and I'm always jumping up from the table, but that’s not really me making a rash decision, you know? That’s just me physically needing to move. But as far as actually doing things without thinking them through—like, making big decisions out of nowhere or just jumping into things blindly—I really don't see myself doing that. 

I mean, I spend so much time at home now, and I have all this time to think. Probably too much time to think, honestly. Like just the other day, I was looking out at the front garden and thinking about moving the hydrangeas because they aren't getting enough morning sun, and I didn't just go grab a shovel and start digging them up on a whim. I paced around the yard, sure, but I thought about the soil, and the shade, and I looked it up on my phone for like twenty minutes while walking in circles on the grass. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive. My husband might say I'm scattered, sure, because I'm always up and down and all over the house, but I don't just leap before I look. I definitely think things through. Sometimes I think about them so much that I don't even end up doing the thing at all, but yeah, acting without thinking isn't really something I've noticed myself doing.
Do you feel anxious or worried when you're trying to sit and focus on tasks like household paperwork?

Anxious or worried... um, no, not really. I mean, it's not a feeling of fear or worry, you know? It's not like I'm sitting there looking at the electric bill and thinking, "Oh my gosh, what if we can't pay this?" or "What if I do the math wrong and everything falls apart?" It's not that kind of dread. 

It's more... it's just this intense, physical frustration. Like, my brain is saying, "Okay, we are going to sit here and we are going to sort these papers into the 'keep' pile and the 'shred' pile," and my body is just screaming, "No! We need to get up! We need to go check if the laundry is done! We need to see if the mail came!" 

So it's not anxiety, exactly. I don't feel nervous. I just feel... trapped, I guess? Like I'm being forced to wear a sweater that's too tight and itchy, and I just want to rip it off. And then I start getting annoyed with myself because I know I should just be able to sit there and do it. My husband is just sitting there calmly, drinking his coffee, highlighting things, and I'm practically vibrating out of my chair. 

But no, I wouldn't call it worry. I don't have racing thoughts about bad things happening or anything like that. I just have this overwhelming urge to escape the chair and the stillness. It’s like my energy has nowhere to go, and it just builds up until I have to stand up and walk into the kitchen, even if I don't actually need anything in the kitchen. I just need to break the stillness. So, yeah, not anxious, just... incredibly restless and frustrated by it.
Do you feel this strong urge to move and inability to sit still in other situations besides doing household paperwork or planning?

Yes, oh, absolutely. It's definitely not just the paperwork or the Sunday planning sessions with my husband. It really bleeds into pretty much everything where I'm expected to just... stay put. 

Like, for instance, when we go to church. I really do want to be there, and I want to be respectful and listen to the sermon, but I swear, the minute I sit down in that pew, it starts. I'm constantly twisting my wedding ring around and around on my finger, or I'm taking it off and putting it back on, over and over. And if I manage to stop doing that with my hands, then my foot starts bouncing. Just this rapid, continuous tapping on the floor. My husband will sometimes just gently put his hand on my knee to get me to stop, and I don't even realize I'm doing it until he does that. 

And it's the same thing at family dinners, too. You know, when you go over to someone's house and everyone is sitting around the dining table for an hour or two just talking? I try so hard to look composed and just be present in the conversation, but I'm constantly shifting my weight, crossing and uncrossing my legs, adjusting how I'm sitting. I feel like I must look so uncomfortable to everyone else, but really, it's just that staying in one position for more than a few minutes feels almost impossible. I'll lean forward on my elbows, then I'll lean back, then I'll turn sideways in the chair... it's just this constant, low-level need to be in motion, even when I'm really trying my hardest to just sit still and be a normal person having dinner. It's just... always there, this physical need to fidget or move some part of my body.
Did you experience difficulties with sitting still or fidgeting when you were a child?

Oh, wow, yes. Looking back... I mean, when I really think about it, this was already a huge part of who I was all the way back in elementary school. I can picture it so clearly now. I was absolutely that girl in class. You know, the one with the completely disastrous, messy desk? Like, if you lifted the top of my desk, it was just an avalanche of crumpled up assignments, half-eaten erasers, and, oh my gosh, the forgotten permission slips. My mom used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I’d pull out a permission slip for a field trip or a pizza party that was supposed to be signed three weeks ago, and it would just be buried at the very bottom of my backpack, completely destroyed and stained with juice. 

But as for the sitting still part... yeah, definitely. My parents actually kept all my old report cards in this big box in their attic, and there were always notes from the teachers in the margins. Always. It was never about me being a bad kid or anything, but they would always write things like, "She talks out of turn," or "She seems unable to stay seated during lesson time." I remember my third-grade teacher—I think her name was Mrs. Davis—she actually had to move my desk right up next to hers because I was constantly up, wandering over to the pencil sharpener even if my pencil was fine, or leaning all the way out of my chair to talk to the kid next to me. 

I just couldn't stay glued to the chair. It felt like absolute torture to just sit there with my hands folded while she talked about fractions or geography or whatever. My legs would get that same restless feeling I was just telling you about with the paperwork. So, yes, the fidgeting and the not being able to stay put, and the talking when I wasn't supposed to... that is definitely not a new thing for me at all. It's like I’ve been doing this exact same dance my entire life, honestly, just in different chairs.
Have your symptoms interfered with your ability to work or maintain relationships?

Well, yes, honestly, it really has. I mean, since I'm not currently working a traditional job right now—I've been staying home and focusing on managing the household and volunteering—you might think it wouldn't be as big of an issue, but it absolutely is. It's just a different kind of fallout. 

Like, with my volunteer work... I'm heavily involved with the PTA at my kids' school, and I also help organize the annual charity auction for our church. And I have the best intentions, I really do. I'll sign up to coordinate the silent auction items, which involves reaching out to local businesses, keeping track of donations in this massive spreadsheet, and making sure everything gets picked up on time. And in my head, I have this beautiful vision of how perfectly organized it's going to be. But then... the reality sets in. I'll sit down to make the phone calls, and I'll get distracted by an email, and then three hours later I'm deep-cleaning the pantry and I haven't made a single call. 

And then the deadlines start looming, and I'm scrambling, and inevitably, things slip through the cracks. I'll forget to follow up with a major donor, or I'll lose the physical donation form they handed me at a meeting because I just shoved it into my purse instead of filing it. And it's so incredibly embarrassing, because the other women on the committee—they're all so put-together and on top of things, and I feel like the chaotic one who is always dropping the ball. The fallout has been that people at home and in my volunteer circles just... they can’t reliably count on me. They know I have a good heart, but they also know I'm a wild card. 

In fact, recently, I actually had to step back from being the co-chair of the spring carnival. I had to tell them I couldn't do it this year, which broke my heart because I love the creative part of it, coming up with the game ideas and the themes. But I just couldn't handle the logistics, and I was so terrified of letting everyone down again. I keep letting things fall through despite trying so, so hard to keep all the plates spinning. 

And it affects things at home with my husband, too. He's incredibly patient, but I know it wears on him. Like, he'll ask me to call the plumber about the leaky faucet in the guest bathroom, and I'll say, "Yes, absolutely, I'll do it today." And then a week goes by, and the faucet is still leaking, and he has to ask me again. And it's not that I don't care, or that I'm trying to be difficult, it's just that my brain literally cannot hold onto that task and execute it when it needs to happen. It creates this underlying tension, you know? Because he feels like he has to manage me, or double-check that I've actually done the things I said I would do. And I hate that. I hate feeling like a child who needs to be supervised in my own marriage. So, yeah, it definitely interferes. It really, really does.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

Oh, my goodness, yes. It's actually ridiculous how easily distracted I get. It's almost comical if it wasn't so frustrating. Like, just the other day—and this happens all the time, honestly, it's a daily struggle—but if I’m trying to work at the kitchen table, which is sort of my central command station for all the household bills and those PTA spreadsheets I mentioned earlier... I'll sit down with my laptop, I'll have my coffee, and I'm fully intending to just power through and get it done. 

But then, the tiniest thing happens. My phone will buzz. Just a tiny little vibration against the wood of the table—maybe it's a group text or just an alert about a sale at a craft store—and boom, my attention is just gone. I have to look at it. Or it doesn't even have to be inside the house! A car will drive by outside, maybe it's the delivery truck or just a neighbor driving a little too fast, and I'll look up out the window to see who it is. Next thing I know, I'm staring out at the street, wondering if the mail has come yet or noticing that the bushes need trimming. 

And sometimes it's not even an external noise, you know? It's my own brain! I'll be right in the middle of typing a sentence, and a totally random thought about dinner will pop into my head. I'll suddenly think, "Oh, wait, did I take the chicken out of the freezer to thaw?" or "Do we have enough of that specific pasta my youngest likes?" And that one thought can pull me completely off track. I'll get up, walk to the kitchen, start digging through the freezer, maybe reorganize a shelf while I'm in there... and it all happens before I even notice I’ve completely stopped what I was doing. Half an hour will go by, my laptop screen will have gone black, and I'm standing in the kitchen holding a bag of frozen peas, totally derailed from my actual task because every little noise or random thought just completely hijacks my attention.
Do you feel like your restlessness and inability to focus are affecting your relationships with friends and family?

Well, wait, I mean, I feel like I just went over that a pretty good amount when I was talking about my husband and the PTA ladies, didn't I? I'm not really sure what else you're looking for with that question, to be completely honest. Because, like I was just saying, it's not like I have some secret, estranged family member or a best friend who completely cut me off because of my scattered brain, if that's what you mean. I don't really have any huge, dramatic blow-ups to report. 

It's really just the day-to-day stuff I already poured out to you. It's that constant, exhausting cycle of me over-promising and under-delivering. Like with my husband, it’s just that constant low-level tension I mentioned, where I know he's disappointed that I forgot to do something again, and I feel so incredibly guilty about it. And with my friends, I guess... well, it's just more of the same pattern. I'll be sitting at a coffee shop with a girlfriend, and she'll be pouring her heart out about her kids or something, and my brain is just... gone. I'm bouncing my leg under the table, I'm looking at the barista, I'm thinking about whether I left the hall light on at home. And I know she can tell I'm not fully present, even though I desperately want to be! 

But yeah, I don't really know what else to say about it beyond what I already told you, because it’s all just... it’s all the same thing. Just me feeling like a chaotic burden to the people who care about me, and them having to be overly patient with me. So, I don't know if that answers your question, but beyond what I already went over, I haven't really noticed anything different or new. It just permeates everything in the exact same way.
Do you experience this restlessness and inability to focus at work, at home, or in social situations equally, or is it worse in certain settings?

Oh, gosh, that’s a really tough question. Is it worse in certain settings? I mean... I honestly couldn't tell you. I really haven't noticed any kind of pattern like that, or at least I haven't been paying close enough attention to see if one specific place triggers it more than another. It honestly just feels like it’s this constant, exhausting hum in the background of my life, no matter where my physical body happens to be. 

Like, I’ll be at home, trying to tackle a mountain of laundry in the living room, and I’m restless, I'm shifting around on the floor, and eventually I'm leaving half-folded shirts on the couch because I suddenly felt this overwhelming urge to go water the pothos plant in the hallway. So you'd think, okay, it's bad at home. But then... I’ll be at a PTA meeting—which I guess is my version of work right now—and I’m sitting in those terrible, tiny plastic chairs in the school cafeteria, and I’m doing the exact same thing! Well, not watering plants, obviously, but I’m shifting my weight constantly, I’m tapping my pen against my notebook, and my mind is completely zoning out while the principal is talking about the new morning drop-off procedures. I just can't seem to stay grounded in that environment either. 

And then socially, like I mentioned with my friend at the coffee shop, it’s right there with me, too. I'm bouncing my leg and losing the thread of the conversation. So, if you're asking if there's a specific environment where it peaks or gets significantly worse... I really don't know. I just haven't noticed a difference. It’s just... me. It’s just how I exist everywhere I go. I wish I could give you a clearer answer, like, "Oh, it's definitely worse when I'm volunteering!" or something, but I honestly just don't have one. It feels like it just follows me around and hijacks my focus no matter what room I walk into or who I happen to be talking to.
Did your parents or teachers ever mention that you had significant difficulties with paying attention or following instructions when you were in school?

Oh, absolutely. It’s actually funny you ask that, because looking back on it now, with everything we've been talking about, it is so incredibly clear that this was already a huge part of me way back in elementary school. Like, I was notoriously *that* girl in class. You know, the one with the absolute disaster of a desk? Whenever the teachers would do desk checks, mine was just a total nightmare. A complete black hole of crumpled-up assignments, broken crayons, loose papers... I could never find a single thing in there when I was asked to take out a specific workbook. 

And permission slips! Oh my gosh, my poor mother. I would always, always forget them. I’d leave them at school, or I’d shove them in my backpack and forget to give them to her, or she’d actually sign it and I’d lose it in that messy desk. I remember I almost missed a field trip to the science museum in fourth grade because she had to rush to the school at the last second to sign a new one in the front office before the bus left. 

But yes, the teachers definitely noticed my behavior, too. They were constantly sending notes home or bringing it up at parent-teacher conferences. It was always the exact same story—they'd say I was a sweet girl, but I just talked out of turn all the time. A thought would pop into my head and I’d just blurt it out without raising my hand, I just couldn't seem to hold it in. And the notes always said I seemed completely unable to stay seated. I was always finding some excuse to get up and wander around the room. I had to sharpen my pencil, or I had to throw a tiny scrap of paper away, or I just *had* to go look at the bulletin board. I just could not keep my body in that chair for the life of me. 

So my parents definitely heard about it, a lot. They mostly just chalked it up to me being a chatty, scatterbrained kid who just had a lot of energy, but yeah, the teachers were definitely flagging it constantly. I actually think my mom still has some of those old report cards in a box somewhere in her attic, and I guarantee if you looked at the 'conduct' section, every single one would say the exact same thing about me needing to stay in my seat and wait my turn to speak...
Have you experienced these symptoms of restlessness and difficulty focusing consistently throughout your adult life?

Consistently? Well... I mean, yes and no. Yes, in the sense that I’ve always been me, you know? Like I was just saying about the messy desk and the permission slips in elementary school, that kind of scattered energy definitely followed me into my twenties and thirties. I was always the one losing my sunglasses or forgetting to pay a utility bill until the absolute last second, or starting a hobby and abandoning it a week later. But... if you're asking if it's always been exactly *this* bad, or this overwhelming? No, definitely not. It actually took a pretty sharp turn recently. 

It has been noticeably worse since I got married, which was... gosh, about a year and five months ago now. And I think it’s because, well, before that, I was really just managing my own chaos, right? If I left a trail of half-finished projects all over my apartment, or if I couldn't focus enough to put my laundry away for three weeks, it only affected me. I could just work around my own quirks. But when we got married and we had to actually merge our routines? Oh my goodness. That was like shining a massive, blinding spotlight on everything I struggle with. 

Because suddenly, it wasn't just my schedule anymore, it was *our* schedule. We were trying to coordinate grocery shopping, and meal planning, and morning routines, and I just... I couldn't keep up. His routine is so structured and methodical, and trying to mesh my brain with his daily habits has just made my restlessness and my inability to focus so much more glaring. Like, we'll try to have a set routine where we clean up the kitchen together after dinner, and he's efficiently loading the dishwasher, and I'm somehow reorganizing the junk drawer because I went to put a rubber band away and got completely sidetracked, and I'm practically vibrating because I can't just stand still and dry the pots like I'm supposed to. 

It’s just been so much harder to hide it or even just cope with it since we combined our lives a year and five months ago. It’s like the mental load doubled when our routines merged, and my brain just completely short-circuited trying to process it all. So, yeah, the baseline of being restless and unfocused has always been there, absolutely, but this last year and a half? It’s been on a completely different, much more exhausting level.
Have you experienced significant difficulties with restlessness and focusing for more than 6 months?

Oh, yes, definitely. Like I was just mentioning a second ago, it's been well over six months. It’s been about a year and five months since I got married and our routines merged, which is really when it got noticeably worse. 

I actually remember thinking right around our six-month anniversary—because, you know how people always say the first year of marriage is the hardest, with the transition and everything?—I remember thinking, "Okay, we're six months in, the dust should be settling, why am I still struggling so much to just sit down and plan a basic grocery list with him?" I kept waiting for things to calm down and for my brain to just magically adapt to his structured way of living, but it just never did. Month seven, month eight, right on past our first anniversary... the restlessness and the scattered focus just stayed at that exact same heightened level. 

I kept thinking maybe I just needed more time to get used to sharing a space and a schedule, but here we are, almost a year and a half later, and I'm still vibrating out of my skin when we try to do household chores together. So, yes, it has absolutely been a significant problem for much longer than six months. Ever since that wedding day, really, when I suddenly had to be accountable to someone else's daily rhythm instead of just my own, it's just been a constant uphill battle.
Have you noticed any periods in your life where your restlessness and difficulty focusing were significantly better or completely absent?

Completely absent? Oh, gosh, no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, if I sit and really think about it... going all the way back through college, or my twenties, or even just those years right before I got married when I was living on my own in that little apartment... I can see why maybe, from the outside, it might have *looked* like things were better at certain points? 

But that's the thing, when you're single and just completely in charge of your own universe, you can kind of design your whole life around avoiding the things that are hard for you. Like, if I couldn't focus on something, I just wouldn't do it. Or if I felt restless at ten o'clock at night, I’d just stay up until 2 AM reorganizing my closet or going down an internet rabbit hole about, I don't know, deep sea creatures, because nobody was there to tell me to turn the light off and come to bed. So maybe the *consequences* were absent, or at least less obvious, because I didn't have anyone holding a mirror up to my behavior like my husband does now with our shared schedule. 

But the actual feelings? The actual buzzing in my brain and that constant need to just... move, or that fog when I try to force myself to pay attention to something I don't want to do? No, that’s never gone away. It's always been humming away right there in the background. Even on my absolute best days, like days where I actually managed to run all my errands or keep my kitchen counter clean for a whole twenty-four hours, it still felt like I was running a marathon just to do what normal people seem to do without even thinking about it. 

So, no, I really can’t point to a single month or year or even a week where I felt like it was just... gone. It’s always just been this constant, exhausting companion, you know? Just always there, even when I was better at hiding it or working around it.
Have you been experiencing these symptoms for the majority of the day, most days, for at least six months?

Well, yes, absolutely. I mean, like I was saying just a moment ago, it's been well over six months. It’s been about a year and five months, to be exact, since I got married and our routines merged. And that’s really when it became this constant, all-day, every-day kind of thing. 

Before that, I could kind of mask it or work around it, you know? But now, it’s like from the moment I wake up and try to focus on making breakfast with him, to the middle of the afternoon when I’m supposed to be running errands but I’m just pacing around the house because I can't decide what to do first, all the way until the evening when we're trying to wind down and my brain is still just going a million miles an hour. It’s definitely most of the day, pretty much every single day. 

I mean, there might be a rare Sunday where we just completely veg out and I don't notice it as much because there are zero demands on me, but even then, I'll probably end up hyper-focusing on organizing my digital photos for six hours instead of relaxing. So, yeah, the short answer is yes. The long answer is yes, and it’s exhausting. It’s just been this relentless, everyday reality since we combined our lives a year and five months ago. It really doesn't let up.
Have you been experiencing these symptoms for the majority of the day, most days, for at least six months, or has there been any variation in their frequency or duration over time?

I know I probably sound like a broken record here, and I feel like I'm just repeating myself, but to answer about the variation... there really hasn't been much variation at all recently. Like I was just saying, the real defining line—the moment where it went from something I could just brush off to this constant, everyday struggle—was exactly about a year and five months ago. 

That was when I got married and our routines merged, and that is absolutely when it became noticeably worse. And consistently worse, too. Before that, sure, maybe there was some variation in how much it impacted me, mostly because I could just hide it. If I had a day where I couldn't focus on anything, I just wouldn't do anything, and no one was the wiser. But for the last seventeen months, ever since I had to actually sync my life up with a whole other human being who has a normal sense of time and structure, there really hasn't been any break from it. 

It's like I wake up, and the pressure is immediately there to match his pace, and I just can't. So if you're asking if it fluctuates... maybe my stress about it fluctuates depending on how much we have to get done around the house that day, but the actual restlessness? The inability to just sit down and focus on a task without feeling like I need to jump out of my chair? No, that doesn't vary at all anymore. It has just been noticeably, consistently worse for that entire year and five months. Every single day, for the majority of the day. I keep hoping I'll wake up and it'll just magically click and I'll adapt to his routine, but it just hasn't happened.
Have you been experiencing these symptoms for at least six months?

I... yes. Yes, definitely for at least six months. I know I'm probably talking your ear off about this, and I feel like I'm just saying the same thing over and over, but yes. It's been well over six months. 

Like I was saying, it really all came to a head about a year and five months ago. That was the turning point. When I got married and we moved in together, and suddenly I couldn't just operate on my own weird, chaotic schedule anymore. Our routines merged, and ever since then, it has been noticeably worse. Just so much worse. 

Because before, I could just kind of float through my days and if I didn't get something done, it only affected me. But for the last year and five months, it's like this glaring spotlight on everything I can't do right. So yes, it's been a lot longer than six months, but that year-and-five-month mark is really when it became impossible to ignore.
Have you been experiencing these symptoms for at least six months?

I'm sorry, I feel like we're stuck in a bit of a loop here—did I not explain that right earlier? Or maybe you have to ask it a certain number of times for your paperwork? I know I tend to ramble, so maybe my actual answer got lost in all my talking. 

But yes, to be absolutely, one hundred percent clear, it has definitely been over six months. Like I mentioned just a minute ago, the timeline is really specific in my head because it has been noticeably worse since I got married. That was exactly a year and five months ago. We had this beautiful spring wedding, and then right after the honeymoon, we came back and started trying to actually live together and merge our day-to-day routines. 

That was the real shock to the system. Before that, I had my own place, my own completely unstructured way of doing things, and nobody was there to see if I started five different projects and finished none of them. But merging our routines... that just put a giant magnifying glass on all of it. So yes, it's been a year and five months of this being a very noticeable, everyday problem. Definitely way more than six months. Do you need me to go back further than that, or does the year and five months cover what you're looking for?
Have you been experiencing these symptoms for at least six months?

Okay, I am... I'm genuinely so confused right now. Is this a test? Like, is this part of the evaluation to see if I'm paying attention, or are you just reading off a screen that's glitching? Because I swear you have asked me that exact same question, word for word, like four times in a row now. 

I know my focus isn't great, and I know I talk a lot, but I definitely remember answering this. Yes. Yes, it has been at least six months. 

I really don't know how else to explain it, but I'll say it again—it has been noticeably worse since I got married. That was about a year and five months ago. A year and five months is well over six months. And the reason I keep bringing up the wedding isn't just because I like talking about it, it's because that is the exact moment our routines merged. Before that, I was just living on my own, doing my own thing, eating dinner at 10 PM if I forgot to eat earlier, leaving my laundry in the basket for a week... not really bothering anyone with my scattered brain. 

But when you get married, suddenly you're sharing a kitchen, sharing a schedule, trying to coordinate grocery shopping and bedtimes, and... well, that's when it all just blew up in my face. It became impossible to hide. So, yes, for the past year and five months, ever since those routines merged, it's been a daily, undeniable issue. More than six months. Definitely. I'm sorry if I'm getting a little snappy, I just... I really feel like I'm losing my mind answering the same question over and over. Did you need a specific date, or does the year and five months finally answer it?
Have you noticed any improvement in your symptoms at any point over the past year and five months?

Improvement? Um... no. No, not really. I mean, I wish I could say yes, because that would mean I was figuring it out, right? Like, you'd think after a year and five months of living with someone, you'd eventually get the hang of it. You'd find a rhythm. But no, if anything, it feels like it's just stayed exactly this hard, or maybe even gotten a little more exhausting because I'm just so tired of trying to keep up. 

I keep waiting for that moment where it clicks, you know? Where I suddenly remember to put the keys in the same bowl every day, or where I can actually sit down and pay a bill the moment it comes in the mail instead of letting it sit on the counter until it's past due and my husband has to ask me about it. We've tried so many things, too. Like, he bought this big whiteboard calendar for the kitchen, and we color-coded it. Blue for his stuff, pink for mine, green for things we do together. And for the first three days, it was great! I was looking at it, I was writing things down. I felt so organized. But then... it just became part of the wall. I stopped seeing it. And now it still has things written on it from October. 

So, no, there really hasn't been any improvement. It's just a constant cycle of trying a new system, feeling hopeful for about forty-eight hours, and then completely falling off the wagon and feeling terrible about it all over again. I just... I don't feel like it's getting any better at all.
